## 2. What Exactly Is MCP Events?

MCP Events is an official MCP extension identified as:

> `io.modelcontextprotocol/events`

It is designed to connect MCP clients with events happening in upstream systems.

Official status (November 2026):

  * Specification proposal: SEP-3415 — Final
  * Extension status: Beta
  * Required MCP protocol revision: `2026-07-28` or later
  * Maintained by: Tasks and Events Working Group
  * Support: Requires explicit client and server opt-in

The central idea is simple.

Instead of repeatedly asking a system whether anything changed, an MCP client can subscribe to specific categories of events.

For example: “Subscribe to high-priority incidents belonging to the payment service.”

When a matching incident occurs, the MCP server delivers an event occurrence to the client. The client then passes that event to the agent runtime, which decides what should happen next.

An important distinction: MCP Events delivers information about events. It does not automatically authorize an AI agent to execute arbitrary actions.

## Questions

### What is MCP Events?

A draft extension to the Model Context Protocol, proposed in SEP-3415, that lets an MCP server notify a client when something happens upstream. Clients can poll, hold a push stream open, or register a signed webhook.

### Does Claude support MCP Events?

Not yet. As of October 2026, Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code don't support it. ChatGPT supports the webhook mode in Work chats.

### Is MCP Events part of the MCP spec?

Not yet. SEP-3415 is an open pull request, and the error codes and some details are still provisional.

What is model context protocol (MCP)?
Date: Tue Oct 28 11:48:34 2025 UTC

Large language models, the engines of many of today's cutting edge AI applications, process and return responses to prompts using training data, whether the task at hand is solving a logic-level problem or writing complex lines of code. LLMs cannot 'naturally' access external databases, content repositories, and third-party applications..
Linking LLMs to external data used to be a manually intensive, case-by-case task. Model context protocol (MCP) is a standard, open source AI protocol that provides a secure environment for LLMs to connect with external databases, tools, software, and services in real-time. It functions as a kind of universal language that enables LLMs to move beyond their training data.
Anthropic, the American AI developer responsible for Claude, released MCP as an open source standard on November 25, 2024. The firm published the documentation and announced MCP in a blog post, drawing an analogy between the MCP protocol and USB Type-C, which helps any device connect to a computer.
Fintech company Block and app development platform Apollo GraphQL were listed as early adopters of MCP. Anthropic has since partnered with developer tool companies like Zed, Replit, Sourcegraph, and Codeium to incorporate MCP in their products for AI-assisted development.
Ever since the release, MCP has received support from across the AI ecosystem. Core AI enterprises such as OpenAI and Google DeepMind adopted MCP within six months of its release. One of the recent MCP initiatives includes the addition of Microsoft, through Copilot Plus PC and Windows AI.

MCP architecture 

MCP is an AI standard that works in a client-server architecture. All the MCP client-server communication takes place at the transport layer through standard input/output (STDIO), HTTP+ security, and server-sent events (SSE) methods.

MCP Host

The MCP host is an AI application or an IDE that contains an LLM. It is a simple interaction point for the user.

MCP client

The MCP client, embedded in the host, converts user requests into a standardized format and sends them to MCP servers. One MCP client can effortlessly connect to "N" MCP servers while maintaining a secure 1:1 connection. Some examples of connection requests include:

MCP server

The MCP server is an independent service, database, or application programming interface (API) that listens to requests from MCP clients and returns them with the requested context, data resources, tools, and capabilities. In simple words, the MCP server converts client requests into actionable steps for the LLM.
The MCP client receives results from the server, performs translation, and passes them back to the LLM. As a result, the LLM gets access to external data or tools.

MCP: The unified advantage

At the beginning of widespread enterprise AI adoption, AI applications were stateless models. But AI users of 2025 demand context across conversations, while AI agents necessitate communication across applications and cloud environments.
By simplifying cross-platform integration, the MCP protocol makes AI even better at decision-making.

Unloading the weight of the N x M problem 

N x M is an infamous problem in AI architecture. N is the number of AI models, and M is the number of tools. Both numbers are ever-growing. Each LLM requires a new custom integration to work with a specific third-party application, where developers manually fetch data from APIs and inject it into LLMs.
Due to the N x M problem, the number of custom integrations grows exponentially. It is no surprise that custom integrations skyrocket the budget and place a significant development load on engineers to seek permissions, debug, and perform whatnot!
"For years, every AI project meant building one-off connectors and custom logic to pass context around," explains Facundo Giuliani, solutions engineering team manager at Storyblok. "MCP changes that by providing a unified standard that fits naturally into composable and MACH architectures. It brings the same modularity and reusability we already expect from modern software development into the AI layer".
MCP is best suited for MACH architectures (Microservices API-First Cloud-Native and Headless), which call for quick, pluggable, and scalable architectures built on third-party tools. Multi-agent orchestration: Agentic AI is not just a typical generative AI chatbot, but an agent that can make decisions and perform real-time tasks to assist humans. Enterprises are heavily invested in deploying such AI agents to automate workloads.
"By standardizing agent-to-agent and agent-to-tool communications, we create a clean interface you can reason about, test, and govern across clouds and vendors," says Randy Bias, VP of Strategy & Technology at Mirantis, a B2B open source cloud computing software and services company.
MCP enables enterprises to deploy multiple AI agents through the MCP pipeline on different business processes. These AI agents collectively work to execute tasks.
Cloud management: The MCP server enables converting natural language into SQL queries. Without non-technical skills, users access databases and manage storage services.
Personalized assistant: MCP enables AI applications to connect agents to client devices, allowing AI agents to interact with common enterprise tools such as Notion, Slack, Google Calendar. This powers more autonomous tasks such as ticket booking, scheduling meetings, messaging, and sharing updates.
Software development: Enterprises have already integrated AI agents into their IDE to improve code generation, debugging, and accuracy reports.
Financial operations: In enterprises, MCP can help applications to fetch and process data from ERP and CRM tools.
Creative solutions: MCP helps AI tools to integrate with web design, 3D animation, and image tools. Figma and Blender MCP servers are two examples.
Startup opportunity: New software or AI applications must build their own MCP server or adapt to existing ones so any MCP client can use them.

What are the risks of MCP?

One of the major problems in the MCP protocol is that the entire foundation is built on trust. For example, MCP servers can be called by anyone, not only LLMs.
"MCP is still a relatively young technology", warns Conor Sherman, CISO-in-residence at cloud security firm Sysdig. Because MCP protocols don't define specific enterprise-grade authentication and authorization mechanisms, businesses need to insulate any MCP use against threats - or face serious security risks.
"The risk is that enterprises will rush to adopt MCP for its interoperability without realising that the 'payload' itself can be weaponized, carrying poisoned instructions or enabling covert exfiltration," explains Sherman.
A recent paper by researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology demonstrates that attackers can embed malicious instructions into MCP servers, which LLMs read through MCP clients. The attack is known as MCP-UPD (Unintended Privacy Disclosure). When LLM uses the malicious data, the hidden code triggers access to private files or results in data theft.
Recent analysis by Backslash Security backs this up, finding approximately half of the 15,000 or more MCP servers being used at the time of publication contain dangerous misconfigurations that put them at risk from hackers.
Incorrect server implementation: When MCP servers are implemented incorrectly, they may expose critical functionalities to AI applications, thus putting enterprise assets at risk.

Prompt injection: LLMs accept malicious prompts written by an attacker. The attack is known as prompt injection. According to a recent analysis by Equixly, 43% of tested MCP implementations contain prompt injection flaws.
MCP functions like a middleware between LLMs and third-party sources, tools, or services. Still, the MCP protocol is in the early stages. Whether MCP becomes an enterprise standard or just another documentation dumped into the vastness of web pages depends on how it is supported.

L26: 
L27: The 【9†ext-events repository†github.com】 contains the full specification for the official Events extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/events`). 【10†SEP-3415】 is Final, and the extension is in Beta. The 【11†Tasks and Events Working Group】 maintains it.
L28: ## modelcontextprotocol/ext-events
L29: 
L30: Full specification and documentation for MCP Events.
L31: 
L32: MCP is request-driven: a user or a model asks, and a server answers. Agents increasingly need to act on things that happen when nobody is asking, such as a new email, a push to a repository or a production incident. MCP Events lets a client subscribe to these upstream events, with arguments, and have an agent react when they occur, even when no user is present.
L33: ## Why not existing notifications?
L34: 
L35: MCP already has notifications such as `notifications/resources/updated` and the `list_changed` family. They don’t cover this use case:
L36:   * No parameters or payload. A notification says that a URI or a list changed. It can’t express “a P1 incident was created for service X”, because there are no subscription arguments, no payload schema and no payload.
L37:   * A live connection is required. Notifications arrive only on an open `subscriptions/listen` stream. A client that isn’t connected receives nothing.
L38:   * No resumption. There is no cursor, so anything that happens during a disconnect is lost, and the client can’t tell that it missed anything.
L39: The deployments that need events also differ. A serverless server can’t hold a connection per subscriber, a client behind NAT can’t receive a callback, and a cost-sensitive client shouldn’t poll. That’s why Events defines three delivery modes, and a server picks the ones that fit each event type.
L40: ## How Events work
L41:   1. Capability negotiation. The server advertises `io.modelcontextprotocol/events` in its `server/discover` capabilities. The client may declare the same identifier in its per-request capabilities.
L42:   2. Discovery. The client calls `events/list`. Each event type has a `name`, an `inputSchema` for subscription arguments, a `payloadSchema` for the data it delivers, and the `delivery` modes it supports.
L43:   3. Subscription. The client subscribes with an event name and arguments, using one of the modes the event type lists. A `null` cursor means “start from now”.
L44:   4. Delivery. Each event arrives as an occurrence: `{eventId, name, timestamp, data, cursor}`. The client stores the cursor after each delivery.
L45:   5. Resumption. After a disconnect or a restart, the client resubscribes with its stored cursor. If the server can’t serve from that position, it says so with `truncated: true`, so the client knows that events were skipped.
L46:   6. Reaction. The client SDK hands each event to the agent runtime, which decides how to react, for example by starting a new agent turn.
L47: ## Delivery modes
L48: 
L49: None of the three modes is mandatory. An event type lists any non-empty subset of them, and the client SDK picks one it can use.
L50: Mode  | Method  | How it works  | Good fit for
L51: --- | --- | --- | ---
L52: Poll  | `events/poll`  | The client asks for new events at the interval the server recommends. The server holds no per-client state.  | Stateless and serverless servers, simple clients
L53: Push  | `events/stream`  | The client holds a long-lived request open, and the server delivers events on it as notifications.  | Local (stdio) servers, clients that stay connected
L54: Webhook  | `events/subscribe`  | The client registers an `https` callback URL, and the server POSTs signed events to it under a renewable TTL.  | Remote servers, clients that can’t hold a connection
L55: SDKs typically prefer webhook when the client has a callback endpoint, then push, then poll. A client can override the choice per subscription.
L56: ## When to use Events
L57: Events are a good fit when your use case involves: Reacting to upstream activity. New messages, repository pushes, payments, incidents or calendar changes that an agent should act on. Unattended agents. Background agents that run when no user is present and need to be woken by something happening. Filtered streams. Subscriptions that narrow a large stream with arguments, such as “P1 incidents for service X” or “email from this sender”.
L58: If the client is waiting for the result of a long-running operation it started itself, use 【12†Tasks】 instead.
L59: ## Cursors and delivery guarantees
L60: 
L61: Cursors are opaque, server-defined positions in the event stream. They make delivery at-least-once when the upstream is durable and the client resumes from its last cursor.
L62:   * Replay is optional per event type. A server returns `cursor: null` for an event type that has no addressable history. The client then always starts from now, and accepts that events during a gap can’t be recovered.
L63:   * Bounded replay. A client can pass `maxAgeMs` with a stale cursor, so that a host that was offline for a week gets at most, say, the last five minutes.
L64:   * Deduplication. `eventId` is stable for an upstream event, so a client can discard duplicates within a subscription.
L65:   * Ordering. Poll and push deliver events in order within a subscription. Webhook ordering is best-effort, and the `timestamp` field orders events.
L66: The client owns its list of subscriptions. There is no server method that lists them, and the client can rebuild server-side state at any time.
L67: ## Security model
L68:   * Payloads are untrusted data. Event payloads come from external systems and can carry prompt injection. Treat them like tool results, and sanitize or sandbox them before they reach a model.
L69:   * Minimal payloads. Servers should send enough to identify and triage an event, such as a sender, subject and ID, and let the client fetch full content with tools.
L70:   * Authorization at every step. The server checks permission at subscribe time, re-checks at delivery time, and terminates the subscription if access is revoked. Receiving an event never authorizes the agent to act: its follow-up tool calls go through normal MCP authorization.
L71:   * Webhook hardening. Deliveries are signed with 【13†Standard Webhooks†www.standardwebhooks.com】 HMAC signatures. Callback URLs must be `https`, the server verifies an endpoint before it delivers to it, and it validates destination IPs to prevent SSRF.
L72: ## Implementation guide
L73: ### For MCP clients
L74: 
L75: 1
L76: 
L77: Declare support
L78: 
L79: Include the extension in the per-request capabilities you send:
L80: 
L81:     `{
L82:       "params": {
L83:         // Other fields...
L84:         "_meta": {
L85:           "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
L86:             "extensions": {
L87:               "io.modelcontextprotocol/events": {},
L88:             },
L89:           },
L90:         },
L91:       },
L92:     }
L93:     `
L94: 
L95: Don’t send `events/*` requests to a server that hasn’t advertised the extension.
L96: 
L97: 2
L98: 
L99: Discover and subscribe
L100: Call `events/list`, validate subscription arguments against each event type’s `inputSchema`, and pick a delivery mode from its `delivery` list.
L101: 
L102: 3
L103: 
L104: Persist cursors
L105: 
L106: Store the latest cursor for each subscription durably, and resume from it after a restart. Treat `truncated: true` as a possible gap, and re-read authoritative state with tools if it matters.
L107: 
L108: 4
L109: 
L110: Deliver events safely
L111: 
L112: Deduplicate by `eventId`, and treat payloads as untrusted before passing them to a model.
L113: ### For MCP servers
L114: 
L115: 1
L116: 
L117: Advertise support
L118: 
L119: Include the extension in your `server/discover` capabilities. Set `listChanged` if you send `notifications/events/list_changed`:
L120: 
L121:     `{
L122:       "result": {
L123:         // Other fields...
L124:         "capabilities": {
L125:           "extensions": {
L126:             "io.modelcontextprotocol/events": {
L127:               "listChanged": true,
L128:             },
L129:           },
L130:         },
L131:       },
L132:     }
L133:     `
L134: 
L135: 2
L136: 
L137: Describe event types
L138: Return each event type from `events/list` with its `inputSchema`, `payloadSchema` and supported `delivery` modes. Evolve schemas additively, and publish a breaking change under a new event name.
L139: 
L140: 3
L141: 
L142: Use upstream identifiers
L143: 
L144: Use the upstream system’s stable event ID as `eventId`, and encode the upstream position in the cursor, so that clients can resume and deduplicate.
L145: 
L146: 4
L147: 
L148: Check authorization
L149: Verify that the principal may subscribe with the given arguments, and terminate subscriptions when access is revoked.
L150: ## Client support
L151: 
L152: MCP Events is an extension to the 【14†core MCP specification】. It requires protocol revision `2026-07-28` or later.
L153: 
L154: See the 【15†client matrix】 for extension support across clients. Events requires explicit opt-in from both client and server.
L155: ## Specification
L156: 
L157: The Events extension is specified in the 【9†ext-events repository†github.com】. It uses the standard MCP 【16†extension negotiation】 mechanism. For the design rationale, see 【10†SEP-3415】.

L194: # Tasks and Events Working Group
L195: 
L196: > ⚠️ Experimental — This repository is an incubation space for the Tasks and Events Working Group. Contents are exploratory and do not represent official MCP specifications or recommendations.
L197: ## Mission
L198: 
L199: The Tasks and Events Working Group exists to define how MCP servers proactively notify clients of state changes. Today, clients learn about server-side updates by polling or holding an SSE connection open. This WG will specify a standardized callback mechanism — webhooks or similar — that lets servers push notifications when new data is available, with defined ordering guarantees that hold across all transports.

L203:   * Specification work: SEPs defining the trigger/callback mechanism, subscription lifecycle, delivery semantics, and event ordering guarantees
L204:   * Reference implementations: SDK components demonstrating server-initiated notifications and client-side callback handling
L205:   * Cross-cutting concerns: Coordination with the Transports WG on transport-specific delivery behavior, and with the Agents WG where task completion notifications intersect with event triggers
L206:   * Documentation: Specification sections covering event-driven patterns and migration guidance from polling-based approaches
L207: ### Out of Scope

L209:   * Changes to the transport wire format or session model (owned by the Transports WG)

You’re right. I looked up **MCP Events**, the new specification, and I had confused it with ordinary MCP notifications. Sorry.

MCP Events lets an MCP server tell an AI agent that something happened **without waiting for a user to ask**. For example, a connected service could report “a new story was saved,” and an agent could then start a task. Clients can receive events by polling, an open stream, or a webhook. The specification is currently a **beta extension**, and both the server and client must support it. [Official MCP Events overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/events/overview)

For your storybook, it could be useful for **background work**—say, an agent reacting when a saved adventure is ready for review. It would not be the right mechanism for stopping the narrator when a child speaks; that immediate interaction already runs through Deepgram’s live speech events. This is my assessment of where the spec fits your app, not a claim made by the spec.

Yes—your instinct is right. **MCP Events only makes sense if your storybook needs to notify an external AI agent**. You would add an MCP server that publishes events, and an MCP client would subscribe to them. The [spec describes that server–client flow](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/events/overview).

For example, an event could say “a child saved an adventure,” letting a separate agent prepare a parent summary. Your current story experience does not need that extra layer. The browser already receives the child’s speech through a live Deepgram connection, which is the right place to handle narrator interruptions.

My suggestion: **don’t add MCP Events for now**. Consider it if you later want ChatGPT or another external agent to react to activity in the storybook while nobody is using the app.

im trying to figure out a use case for an external agent

The strongest use case I see is a **parent’s story companion**.

When a child finishes and saves an adventure, your storybook could send an MCP Event to an external agent. The agent could prepare a short note for the parent: what the child invented, which characters they liked, and an idea for continuing the story together. The parent would choose whether to use it.

That gives the external agent a clear job **outside the live storytelling session**. It can react after a story is saved, while the child’s conversation stays fast and focused.

I’d only build this if you want the storybook to connect to an agent the parent already uses, such as ChatGPT. If the recap would appear only inside your own app, a normal background job would be simpler than an MCP server.
